title: The Empty Corner of the Station
passage: At a small train station near Haru's town, there was an empty corner beside the ticket gate. People usually walked past it without noticing. One winter, the town asked local students to suggest ways to use the space. Some students wanted vending machines, while others suggested a large advertisement board. Haru's group proposed something different: a small waiting area with local information and a bench. Their idea came from watching older passengers who sometimes stood near the wall while waiting for rides. The group first measured the space and counted how many people passed through the station at different times of day. They found that the station was busiest in the morning, but the corner was most useful in the afternoon, when people waited longer for buses or family members. The students also interviewed passengers. Some wanted a place to sit, while visitors said they often had trouble finding information about nearby parks, shops, and walking routes. The town liked the proposal but explained that the budget was limited. The students therefore changed their plan. Instead of buying a new digital display, they designed a simple wooden information board that volunteers could update. A local carpenter offered leftover wood, and an art club painted a map. The town paid only for a strong bench and weather-resistant materials. After the waiting area opened, Haru's group returned to observe it. They noticed that the bench was used often, but the map was sometimes blocked by people standing nearby. The students moved one sign and added a small arrow on the floor. They also found that tourists asked the same three questions repeatedly, so they added answers directly to the board. Haru had imagined that good design meant having a clever idea at the beginning. The project taught him something else. A useful place is created through observation, testing, and small corrections. The first plan does not need to be perfect if people are willing to watch how it is actually used. Months later, the station manager told the students that passengers had begun leaving notes with suggestions for new local information. The empty corner had become more than a place to wait; it had become a small connection between the station and the town.
translation: 春の町の小さな駅には、改札の横に誰も気に留めない空きスペースがありました。冬に町が活用案を募集し、自動販売機や広告板などの案が出る中、春のグループは地元情報を置いた小さな待合スペースを提案しました。高齢の乗客が迎えを待ちながら壁際に立っている姿を見たことがきっかけでした。生徒たちはまず場所を測り、時間帯ごとの通行人数を調べました。朝が最も混雑する一方、午後にはバスや家族を待つ人が長く滞在することが分かりました。利用者への聞き取りでは、座る場所が欲しいという声と、観光客から近くの公園や店、散歩道の情報が分かりにくいという声が出ました。予算が限られていたため、新しいデジタル表示ではなく、ボランティアが更新できる木製案内板に変更しました。地元の大工が余った木材を提供し、美術部が地図を描き、町は丈夫なベンチなど最低限の費用だけを負担しました。完成後に観察すると、ベンチはよく使われるものの地図が人に隠れる問題が見つかり、看板の位置や床の矢印を調整しました。また観光客が同じ質問を繰り返すため、その答えも案内板に加えました。春は良いデザインとは最初から賢い案を出すことだと思っていましたが、観察し、試し、少しずつ直すことが大切だと学びました。数か月後には利用者自身が新しい地元情報の提案を残すようになり、空きスペースは単なる待合場所ではなく、駅と町をつなぐ場所になっていました。

title: Why the Garden Needed Fewer Plants
passage: Rina joined the school gardening club because she loved flowers. During her first year, the club tried to make every corner of the school garden colorful. Members planted many kinds of flowers close together, believing that more plants would make the garden more beautiful. For a few weeks, the result looked wonderful. By early summer, however, problems appeared. Some plants grew quickly and covered smaller ones. Others became weak because they received too little sunlight or air. Watering also took a long time, and club members often disagreed about which areas needed attention first. The adviser did not tell them what to do. Instead, she asked them to record what was happening. The students measured sunlight in different areas, noted how quickly the soil dried, and checked which flowers attracted insects. They discovered that several plants were competing for the same space, while a few stronger plants were doing well with very little care. Rina was surprised when the adviser suggested removing some healthy plants. It felt wrong to take out flowers that were not sick. Yet the club decided to test the idea in one section. They moved some plants to pots and left more space between the remaining ones. A month later, the test area required less water and had fewer damaged leaves. Bees and butterflies could move more easily between flowers, and students had space to pull weeds without stepping on plants. The club then redesigned the rest of the garden. They used fewer species in each area and chose plants according to sunlight and soil conditions. The garden looked less crowded, but the colors were clearer because each group of plants could be seen. The students also spent less time solving emergency problems and more time observing seasonal changes. Rina learned that caring for something does not always mean adding more. Sometimes improvement comes from reducing competition and giving each part enough space. She later noticed the same idea in other situations. A schedule with too many activities can become hard to manage, and a poster with too many messages can be difficult to read. The garden taught her that limits are not always a weakness. They can help people decide what matters most and create conditions in which the remaining parts can grow better.
translation: 里奈は花が好きで園芸部に入りました。最初の年、部員たちは学校の庭をできるだけ色鮮やかにしようと、たくさんの種類の花を狭い場所に植えました。最初はきれいでしたが、夏になると成長の速い植物が小さな植物を覆い、日光や風が足りず弱るものが出てきました。水やりにも時間がかかり、どこを優先するかで意見が分かれました。顧問は答えを教える代わりに、まず状況を記録するよう求めました。生徒たちは日当たり、土の乾き方、昆虫が集まる花などを調べ、いくつもの植物が同じ空間を奪い合っていることに気づきました。顧問が健康な植物を一部取り除く案を出したとき、里奈は驚きました。しかし一角で試しに植物を鉢へ移し、間隔を広げると、一か月後には水の量が減り、葉の傷みも少なくなりました。ハチやチョウも動きやすくなり、除草もしやすくなりました。そこで庭全体を見直し、場所ごとに種類を絞り、日当たりや土に合う植物を選びました。以前ほど密集していませんが、むしろ色のまとまりがはっきりしました。里奈は、世話をすることは必ずしも何かを足すことではなく、競争を減らし十分な空間を与えることも改善につながると学びました。そして、予定を詰め込みすぎると管理が難しくなることや、ポスターに情報を入れすぎると読みにくくなることにも同じ考えが当てはまると気づきました。制限は弱点ではなく、大切なものを選び、残したものをよりよく育てるための条件にもなるのです。

title: The Bus Stop Experiment
passage: A bus stop near Kota's school was crowded every afternoon. Students formed a long line, but when the bus arrived, the line often became unclear. Some people moved forward from the side, and others could not tell where the end of the line was. Complaints increased, yet no one was sure whether the problem came from rude behavior or from the design of the space. For a social studies project, Kota's group decided to observe the stop for one week. They drew a simple map and marked where people stood. They found that the line was straight at first but bent around a bicycle parking area when it became longer. New arrivals then had difficulty seeing the true end of the line. The group also noticed that the timetable was placed near the front. People who only wanted to check the schedule had to walk through the waiting passengers, which made the crowd even less organized. The students shared their observations with the bus company. They did not accuse passengers of behaving badly. Instead, they suggested two small changes: moving a copy of the timetable farther from the boarding point and placing three temporary floor markers to show the direction of the line. The company agreed to test the idea for two weeks. The result was not perfect, but the line became easier to understand. Fewer people entered from the side, and those checking the schedule no longer had to cross the queue. The students then asked passengers for comments. Several people said the markers were useful, but one older passenger found them difficult to see on rainy days. The group suggested adding a small standing sign as well. Kota was interested in how the project changed his view of public problems. At first, he had assumed that people simply needed to follow rules more carefully. Observation showed that the environment itself could make good behavior easier or harder. Clear information, visible paths, and thoughtful placement could prevent confusion before it began. The group wrote in its final report that rules still mattered, but design could support those rules. Kota began noticing similar examples elsewhere: arrows in hospital halls, colored lines at stations, and separate doors for entering and leaving. He realized that many smooth daily activities depend on quiet design choices that people barely notice when they work well.
translation: 光太の学校近くのバス停は毎日午後になると混雑し、バスが来ると列が崩れがちでした。横から前へ入る人がいたり、最後尾が分からなかったりし、苦情も増えていました。しかし原因がマナーなのか場所のつくりなのかは分かりませんでした。社会科の課題で光太たちは一週間観察し、人が立つ位置を地図に記録しました。列は短い間はまっすぐですが、長くなると駐輪場を避けて曲がり、新しく来た人から最後尾が見えなくなることが分かりました。また時刻表が乗車位置の近くにあるため、確認だけしたい人が列の中を横切り、さらに混乱が起きていました。生徒たちは乗客を責めるのではなく、時刻表の写しを少し離れた場所に置き、床に三つの目印を付ける案をバス会社へ提案しました。二週間の試験では、完全ではないものの列は分かりやすくなり、横入りも減り、時刻確認の人も列を横切らなくなりました。高齢者から雨の日は床の印が見にくいという意見が出たため、小さな立て看板も提案しました。光太は、公共の問題を『人がもっと規則を守ればよい』とだけ考えていた自分に気づきます。観察すると、環境そのものが良い行動をしやすくも、しにくくもしていました。分かりやすい情報や動線の工夫は混乱を事前に減らせます。規則は必要ですが、デザインがその規則を支えることもできます。病院の矢印、駅の色分けされた線、入口と出口を分けた扉などにも同じ考えがあり、日常がスムーズに動く背景には、うまく働いているときほど目立たない小さな設計があるのだと光太は理解しました。

title: A Map Made by Walking
passage: Nana's class received an unusual geography assignment. Instead of studying only a printed map, students had to walk around their neighborhood and create a map showing how the area felt to a person on foot. At first, Nana did not understand the difference. A normal map already showed roads, parks, and buildings. What else was there to record? Her group began by walking from the school to the public library. They soon noticed details that were missing from the printed map. One sidewalk became very narrow near a bridge. A crossing took a long time because the signal changed slowly. A small path through a park was shorter than the main road, but it became muddy after rain. They also found places where shade made walking comfortable in summer and corners where cars were difficult to see. The group decided to use symbols for these experiences. A blue mark showed a comfortable path, a red triangle showed a place that required care, and a green line showed a route with trees or shade. They walked the same route at different times and discovered that the experience changed. A quiet street in the morning became crowded when students returned home, while a sunny path became easier to walk in the late afternoon. When the maps were presented, each group had recorded different things. One group focused on wheelchair access, another on places where younger children might feel unsafe, and another on benches and public toilets. The teacher explained that maps are not neutral copies of reality. Every map selects information according to its purpose. A driving map, a disaster map, and a tourist map may show the same town in different ways because users need different information. Nana's group gave its walking map to the community center. A staff member said it could help new residents who wanted to explore the area without a car. Nana was proud, but she also understood the limits of their work. Their map represented only a few days and the experiences of a small group of students. Conditions could change with seasons, construction, or weather. The assignment taught her to ask two questions whenever she looked at a map: what information is included, and whose needs does it serve? She realized that understanding a place requires both a view from above and attention to what people experience on the ground.
translation: 奈々のクラスには少し変わった地理の課題が出ました。印刷された地図を見るだけでなく、地域を実際に歩き、『歩く人にとってどう感じる場所か』を示す地図を作るのです。最初は普通の地図と何が違うのか分かりませんでしたが、学校から図書館まで歩くと、地図にはない多くの情報に気づきました。橋の近くで歩道が急に狭くなる場所、信号待ちが長い横断歩道、近道だが雨の後はぬかるむ公園の道、夏に日陰が気持ちよい場所、車が見えにくい角などです。班は、歩きやすい道、注意が必要な場所、木陰のある道を色や記号で示しました。時間帯を変えて歩くと、朝は静かな道が下校時には混雑するなど、同じ場所でも状況が変わることも分かりました。発表では、車いす利用者の移動に注目した班、小さな子どもの安全を考えた班、ベンチや公衆トイレを記録した班など、それぞれ違う地図になりました。先生は、地図は現実をそのまま写すものではなく、目的に応じて情報を選んでいると説明しました。車用、防災用、観光用では同じ町でも必要な情報が異なります。奈々たちの地図は地域センターに渡され、新しい住民の散歩にも役立つと言われました。ただし奈々は、自分たちの地図も数日間の少人数の経験にすぎず、季節や工事、天気で変わるという限界にも気づきました。以来、地図を見るときには『何が載っているか』『誰の必要に応えるものか』を考えるようになりました。場所を理解するには、上から見る視点と、地上で人が感じる経験の両方が必要なのです。

title: The Quiet Ten Minutes
passage: Every afternoon, the student council office became noisy. Members arrived from different clubs, asked questions, searched for papers, and tried to finish several tasks at once. Meetings often began late because nobody was sure what needed to be done first. Mei, the council secretary, suggested an experiment. For the first ten minutes after school, nobody would hold a meeting. Instead, each person would quietly check the task board, prepare necessary materials, and write one clear goal for the day. Some members thought the rule would waste valuable time. They wanted to start discussing problems immediately. Mei asked them to try it for one week before deciding. On the first day, the room felt strangely silent. One student found that a form he planned to discuss had already been answered by a teacher. Another noticed that two members were preparing the same poster. Because they checked the task board first, they divided the work before the meeting began. By the third day, meetings were starting earlier and ending sooner. The group also added a small section to the board called Waiting For. Tasks that could not continue until someone gave information were placed there. This stopped members from repeatedly asking about work that was temporarily blocked. At the end of the week, the council compared the number of unfinished tasks with the previous week. The difference was not huge, but members reported feeling less rushed. More importantly, they could explain what they had accomplished each day. Mei pointed out that the ten quiet minutes did not reduce work time; they prevented some work from being repeated or started without the right information. The council kept the practice but made it flexible. Before special events, when urgent decisions were necessary, they shortened the quiet period. This taught Mei another lesson: a useful routine should support a goal, not become a rule that people follow without thinking. The success of the experiment came from creating a short pause between arriving and acting. That pause gave everyone time to see the whole situation before choosing the next step. Mei later used the same habit while studying. Before opening a textbook, she spent a few minutes deciding exactly what she wanted to finish. She found that a small amount of planning often saved more time than it cost.
translation: 毎日の放課後、生徒会室は騒がしくなっていました。さまざまな部活から来たメンバーが質問し、書類を探し、複数の作業を同時に始めるため、会議も遅れがちでした。書記の芽衣は、最初の十分間は会議をせず、各自が静かに作業表を確認し、必要な資料を準備し、その日の目標を一つ書く方法を提案しました。時間の無駄だという意見もありましたが、一週間だけ試すことにしました。初日、一人は話し合う予定だった書類にすでに先生の回答があることに気づき、別の二人は同じポスターを重複して作ろうとしていることに気づきました。三日目には会議の開始が早まり、終了も早くなりました。さらに『返答待ち』という欄を作り、誰かの情報が来るまで進められない仕事を分けたことで、止まっている仕事について何度も確認する無駄も減りました。一週間後、未完了の仕事数が劇的に減ったわけではありませんが、メンバーは以前ほど急かされる感覚がなく、その日に何を終えたか説明しやすくなりました。静かな十分間は作業時間を奪うのではなく、重複や情報不足のまま始める作業を防いでいたのです。ただし特別行事前など緊急時には短縮することにしました。芽衣は、習慣は目的を助けるために使うもので、考えず守る規則にしてはいけないとも学びました。到着してすぐ動く前に短い間を置くことで、全体を見て次の行動を選べます。芽衣は勉強でも同じ方法を使い、教科書を開く前に数分だけ『何を終えるか』を決めるようになりました。少しの計画が、それ以上の時間を節約することがあると分かったのです。

title: Before Reading the Labels
passage: During a school trip, Taku visited a small local museum. One room surprised him because several objects were displayed without explanation cards. There was an old wooden tool, a metal box, and a strange glass bottle. Students were asked to guess what the objects had been used for before reading any information. Taku first thought the activity was childish. He wanted the correct answers immediately. However, as his group looked closely, their guesses became more thoughtful. They examined scratches, handles, weight, and shape. One student suggested that the wooden tool had been used in farming because soil remained in a narrow crack. Another thought the metal box might have carried food because it had a tight lid. The museum guide listened without saying who was right. She asked the students to explain what evidence supported each idea. After ten minutes, the guide gave them the labels. Some guesses were correct, while others were not. The metal box, for example, had carried tools rather than food. Yet Taku noticed that the wrong guesses were still useful because they had forced the group to pay attention to details they would otherwise have ignored. In the next room, every object had a full label. This time, Taku caught himself reading the text before really looking at the objects. He understood why the first room had been designed differently. Information can help us understand what we see, but it can also cause us to stop observing for ourselves. At the end of the visit, students were asked to choose one object and write both an observation and an interpretation. Taku chose a worn school bag from many decades ago. His observation was that one side of the handle was smoother than the other. His interpretation was that the owner may have carried it in the same hand every day. He could not prove that idea, but he could separate what he saw from what he believed it might mean. The guide said this difference was important in museums, science, and even daily life. People often mix facts with explanations without noticing. Taku left the museum with fewer facts memorized than he had expected, but with a new habit: look first, describe carefully, and only then decide what the evidence might mean.
translation: 校外学習で拓が訪れた小さな郷土博物館には、説明札が付いていない展示室がありました。古い木製道具、金属箱、不思議なガラス瓶などを見て、説明を読む前に用途を推測する活動です。最初、拓は子どもっぽいと思い、すぐ正解を知りたがりました。しかし観察を続けるうち、班の推測は具体的になりました。傷、持ち手、重さ、形を調べ、木の道具の隙間に土が残っているから農作業用ではないか、金属箱はふたが密閉できるから食べ物を運んだのではないか、などと考えました。案内人は正誤を言わず、『どんな証拠があるか』を説明させました。後で説明札を見ると、正しい推測も間違いもあり、金属箱は食べ物ではなく工具を入れる物でした。それでも拓は、間違った推測にも意味があったと気づきます。答えを先に読んでいたら見逃していた細部を観察できたからです。次の部屋ではすべてに詳しい説明があり、拓は物そのものを見る前に文章を読んでいる自分に気づきました。情報は理解を助ける一方、自分で観察することを止めさせる場合もあります。最後に、生徒は一つの展示物について『観察した事実』と『そこからの解釈』を別々に書きました。拓は古い学生かばんを選び、持ち手の片側だけが滑らかなことを事実として、持ち主が毎日同じ手で持ったのかもしれないと解釈しました。証明はできませんが、見たものと意味づけを分けることができます。案内人は、この区別は博物館だけでなく科学や日常生活でも大切だと話しました。拓は大量の知識より、『まず見て、丁寧に記述し、その後で意味を考える』という新しい習慣を持ち帰りました。
